event_name: NED Talks Tom Lea Mural Discussion
event_description: <p>Trudy Lewis is a retired public-school teacher. She spent 39 years teaching AP U.S. and European history as well as International Baccalaureate History of the Americas in Waco, Midland, and Odessa. While teaching in Odessa, she regularly took students to visit Tom Lea’s 1940 Stampede mural in the post office. Her teaching had such an impact that one student later composed a musical piece inspired by Stampede. In 2014, she presented at the Smithsonian American Art Museum conference on Tom Lea’s New Deal murals, helping forge an historic agreement between the U.S. postal service and the Odessa Council for the Arts and the Ellen Noel Museum to restore and care for Stampede. For the first time, the U.S. Postal Service allowed a community to restore federal property and move the mural to a safe environment at the Ellen Noel Art Museum. Trudy is married to Tryon Lewis, and they have two grown daughters.</p>\n

event_description: <p>Texans love Big Bend National Park, but as it grows in popularity, are the things they love at risk? Former national park superintendent Bob Krumenaker will talk about the grassroots Keep Big Bend Wild (KBBW) initiative, whose goal is to guarantee that the park’s most important asset – its wild, open spaces – will be protected in perpetuity into the future. KBBW is building a widespread coalition of support for a long-dormant effort to see the still-undeveloped wild lands of Big Bend National Park away from the existing roads and facilities be protected as federal wilderness, something only Congress can enact. It’s the best way to protect the park’s natural and cultural resources, wildlife, night skies and natural sounds for future generations while maintaining the facilities and access today’s visitors enjoy. KBBW is working with the NPS to build the public support essential to show our Congressional delegation that that this protection is something Texans want. Wilderness is not a partisan issue and has been championed by people of all political parties. Come, learn about the history and context of this initiative, and be part of a discussion of how you can help to Keep Big Bend Wild.</p>\n

event_description: <p>Come out and join us for our Artist Reception for Loca Artist John Etheridge. John Etheridge was often encouraged by family, teachers, and friends to develop his artistic abilities. In youth, John’s father introduced him to nature through landscape and wildlife. John grew up camping, hiking, canoeing, hunting, and fishing which cemented his lifelong love of nature. John and his two brothers were raised in Dallas, and the family made frequent trips to the Davis Mountains and surrounding areas. John made a living as a graphic designer for over 47 years but continued to practice painting and drawing as time permitted. John is now able to devote his creative time and energy to portraying the landscape and wildlife he loves. After 4 years in the Navy and 7 years in Dallas, John and his wife moved to Odessa. John mostly does representational work in oil, acrylic, watercolor, and graphite pencil, but he also does two and three-dimensional abstracts focusing on form, texture, and color.</p>\n

event_description: <p>He began his career at the University of Arkansas at Little Rock (UALR) Planetarium where he started as a student assistant and worked my way up to Assistant Director from 1987 to 1999. While working there he did many things including being in charge of the NASA Educator Resource Center and gave countless numbers of programs to every kind of group imaginable. He taught Astronomy Classes and Labs for the Department of Physics & Astronomy and was Instrumental in building a 24 inch mobile telescope which spent a lot of its time at Pinnacle Mountain State Park. During his time at the University of Arkansas at Little Rock, he developed several image processing laboratory experiments for the Physics and Astronomy Department’s Astronomy labs. He worked with Dr. Al Grauer in producing and teaching an Intermediate Astronomy class and lab which dealt with image processing on Unix workstations and working with real astronomical data. He worked with the UALR Geology and Science Teacher Education departments and presented programs and workshops for their students. He became a Jet Propulsion Laboratory Ambassador to Jupiter which turned into the Jet Propulsion Laboratory Solar System Ambassador for Arkansas. Currently, he is a retired Planetarium Director, Astronomy Educator and the President of the West Texas Astronomers which is the local Astronomy club. He continues to be a NASA Solar System Ambassador for Texas, and also assisted with the re-opening of the Odessa High School Observatory.</p>\n

event_description: <p>This installation by local artist Susan Enseñat May will include intriguing automatons, photos, and paintings of all sorts of creatures that fly. The AutoMayTons are interactive contraptions that you crank to cause wings to flap and bodies to rotate, jump, or move, mimicking motions found in nature for creatures like owls, bats, butterflies, dragonflies, and more. These creatures, however, are fantastical and created from unusual objects, paper, wire, and recycled materials with a definite steampunk influence. Paintings are in different mediums, with some being realistic and others fantastical. Photos are of flying creatures, both small and large, mostly from our unique West Texas ecoregion with a few from other parts of the state of Texas or the U.S. There is plenty to enjoy for folks of all ages! On display from July-September. Artist Reception August 19 from 6 PM-7:30 PM.</p>\n

event_description: <p>November 14 6PM-7:30PM She was born and raised in Amarillo, Texas where she developed a love for horses, other animals and the outdoors. She is a realistic artist who paints mainly in oils. Her passion for the outdoors and animals which is reflected in her paintings. She varies subject matter but often paint Southwestern and Western scenes. She enjoys painting commissioned pieces of clients\' dogs and other pets. Her photography background has helped to enhance her painting skills. Not only has it helped her to see and compose scenes better, but she able to gather useful information in photographs and take this back to the studio. She then creates a painting using numerous photographs as reference material.</p>\n

event_description: <p>Join us from for the Artist Reception for Joe Hernandez. His bows will be in the gallery from January - March. Joe "Eddie" Hernandez, AKA Loco Pony, was born and raised in Marfa, a small community in far West Texas. After high school he attended Angelo State University in San Angelo. He received his teaching certificate in 1971 and taught school in Odessa for a total of 17 years. As a youngster, he was fascinated with bows and arrows and always had a slingshot in his back pocket. The love for the outdoors and hunting were factors in his desire and passion to learn how to make traditional bows. This included making replicas of primitive bows and arrows. He has hunted black bear in Virginia with his bow for the last 14 years. In March of 2009, he answered an ad in a primitive archery magazine. Ed Scott, a renowned bowyer was advertising bow making classes in Grant, NM. He attended his "one on one" bow making class and learned how to use numerous woods to make traditional bows. These include Osage "bois d arc", hickory, oak, yew, ash and many more. He also utilizes bamboo. In 2010, he went back to work with Ed Scott to learn how to make a "horn bow". Using horns of a Gemsbock deer, he made a unique, beautiful, and functional horn bow. The process takes 6 months to finish a bow. He teaches bow making classes in his shop in Odessa. We can make a bow in a weekend, or we can make one that takes months to complete. My traditional bows will be on display at the Sibley Nature Center in Midland during the first quarter of 2026.</p>\n

event_description: <p>Talon Cress is an artist and freelance graphic designer based in Odessa, Texas. He is a graduate of the University of Texas Permian Basin, where he earned dual bachelor’s degrees in art and organismal biology. Talon has worked across a range of media, including graphite, charcoal, pen & ink, acrylic paint, printmaking, and ceramic sculpture. His practice has been shaped over a long spanning connection to art and a passion for observing and depicting the natural world, particularly the beauty, scale, and individuality of landscapes that offered a sense of grounding during the 2020 pandemic. It was during his time at UTPB that he developed a distinct voice, using his work as a means of personal and conceptual exploration. His work focuses on two central themes, freedom and constraint. A deep appreciation for nature and the boundless possibility it represents as well as the forces that shape and limit human experience, including injury, employment, religion and mortality. Through this contrast, Talon explores transformation, identity, and the individual’s role within a broader, ever-changing world.</p>\n

event_description: <p>Rose Wilhoyt 12 PM - 1 PM Rose is an alumna of Angelo State University, where she graduated with a Bachelor\'s of Science in Biology in 2019. She spent her undergraduate career volunteering and working for the Angelo State Natural History Collections, which nurtured her love of the collections today. Rose did odd jobs throughout the collections, from working "the bug colony" to data entry to specimen preparations, and even dressing up in costume for outreach events. As a student, she learned from her predecessors Marcia Revelez and Dianna Krejsa, as well as from Drs. Dowler and Dixon during their month-long Natural History courses taught abroad in Europe, where she was able to see examples of some of the world\'s most renowned natural collections. Rose began in this position as Collections Manager in January 2024, and she\'s happy to share what she has learned thus far, and the importance of collections in general.</p>\n

event_description: <p>Join us for a FREE teacher workshop at Sibley Nature Center. High School/Middle School/Elementary (6hours) Join us and other area Museums and Education Directors to learn more about area Museums, Nature Centers, Programs, Outreach, and Field Trip Opportunities here in West Texas. We will be joined by The Petroleum Museum, Museum of the Southwest, Ellen Noel Art Museum, Chihuahuan Desert Nature Center, and the Bush Family Home. (Others TBA) We will begin the day with a Sibley Field Trip outline, complete with a nature hike, feeding ducks, stopping in the education garden, and museum. After Lunch we will meet the rest of our presenters in the AC, inside the auditorium and Llano Room. Lessons are TEKS-aligned and fun! Sibley Nature Center is a TEA-Approved Provider. Participants will receive 6 CEU/CPEs for this workshop.  </p>\n
